name: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
title: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
answer: Obligation and service level tracking is the practice of identifying, recording, and monitoring the promises a contract creates, such as delivery dates, payment terms, uptime commitments, and notice periods, and then checking performance against those promises over the life of the agreement. In the AI lawyer context, this sits inside contract lifecycle management and algorithmic drafting because the same structured data that lets software generate clauses can also be used to extract obligations and turn them into tracked items. The scope includes both affirmative duties to do something and negative duties to refrain, as well as service levels that define acceptable performance thresholds. It is distinct from general contract storage because it focuses on ongoing performance rather than the signed document itself.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Obligation and service level tracking runs on contract repositories that store text and metadata, extraction pipelines that pull obligation language from agreements, and scheduling or workflow engines that trigger reviews, alerts, and escalations. The infrastructure typically includes a clause library or playbook that maps common obligation types to standard fields, an integration layer that connects to calendars, ticketing systems, or billing platforms, and a dashboard for status reporting. Because many contracts are legacy scans or PDFs, optical character recognition and text normalization are often part of the stack before extraction can happen. The system may run in a law firm or corporate legal department environment, with access controls separating matter teams.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first defining an obligation model, usually a set of categories such as payment, delivery, renewal, audit, and service level, then applying rules or machine learning to find the relevant sentences and their dates, parties, and thresholds. Human reviewers confirm or correct extracted obligations, especially where language is conditional or cross-referenced. Once obligations are recorded, the system compares actual performance data, such as invoices, support tickets, or uptime logs, against the contractual standard and flags deviations. Algorithmic drafting feeds back into this method by generating clauses with consistent, machine-readable obligation language so future tracking is easier.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on who may change an obligation record, what evidence supports a performance determination, and how disputes about missed service levels are handled. The extracted obligation is not the contract itself, so the system must preserve a link to the source clause and the version of the agreement in force at the relevant time. Access controls should prevent business teams from altering contractual thresholds without legal review, and audit logs should show when an obligation was added, edited, or marked satisfied. Risk arises when tracking is incomplete or wrong, because a missed renewal or unnoticed service credit can create liability or waive a right, so the provenance of each tracked item matters more than the dashboard summary.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Obligation and service level tracking is moving toward continuous monitoring where contract data connects directly to operational systems and performance is assessed in near real time rather than through periodic manual review. Algorithmic drafting is likely to produce more standardized obligation clauses that are designed for extraction, reducing the need for post-signature interpretation. The next step is probably tighter coupling between obligation records and dispute or remediation workflows, so a service level breach can trigger a credit request, a cure notice, or an escalation path without a person re-reading the contract. Over time, the distinction between contract drafting, obligation tracking, and performance management may blur into a single lifecycle record.
sections.heading: Where it is going
